title: Trishanku's stars and the Gayatri's last word
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hookLine: a sage forces a king into the sky, then leaves a prayer that only asks
carry: the gayatri doesn't force: may he stir our minds
tomorrow: a peace chant built for exactly two people. which two?

lines: A KING WANTS HEAVEN IN HIS BODY.
A SAGE LIFTS HIM BY FORCE.
cards: Halfway up his long climb from king to sage, Vishvamitra met a king named Trishanku with a strange wish: to go to heaven in his own body. Vasishtha had refused him, and Vasishtha's sons had cursed him for asking again.
In the Ramayana's telling, Vishvamitra takes pity. He starts a sacrifice, and when the gods won't come, he lifts Trishanku into the sky by the power of his own tapas, his fierce discipline.
Indra, king of the gods, shoves him back: go down. Trishanku falls headfirst, crying for help. Vishvamitra shouts: stop!
And he starts making new stars, a second heaven, by force. The gods give way. Trishanku stays up there, upside down, shining, stuck between earth and heaven.

teach.b: Now set that story beside the verse the same man is remembered for: tat savitur varenyam, bhargo devasya dhimahi, dhiyo yo nah prachodayat.
The last word, prachodayat, joins pra-, forward, to a verb meaning to urge on, and it's said as a wish: may he stir.

teach.h: WE HOLD IN MIND. HE STIRS.
teach.b: Whole: we hold in mind that worth-choosing radiance of the god Savitr; may he stir our thoughts. The people's verb is dhimahi: we hold in mind. The stirring belongs to the god.
Nobody in the Gayatri forces anything.
Many teachers read the man and the verse together: the sage who once pushed a king into the sky by sheer will is remembered for a prayer that only asks.
That's the teaching inside the Gayatri: the light that wakes a mind isn't seized; it's asked for, and given. Families pass it on the same way.
At the upanayana, the sacred thread ceremony, a boy, and in some families today a girl, receives the Gayatri from a teacher or a father, often said close to the ear.
Many then say it at sandhya, the prayers at the day's turning points, facing the sun. Here's where it meets a life now.
Most of us push at what we want the way Vishvamitra pushed Trishanku. The Gayatri starts the day by asking for one thing first: a mind lit enough to see what's worth pushing for.
Priya's dad says it every morning; she'll keep it for home and find a peace chant for the stage.

how: Many Hindus receive the Gayatri at the upanayana, the sacred thread ceremony, and say it at sandhya, the prayers at dawn, noon and dusk, often facing the sun. Tradition names Vishvamitra as its seer.

games.q: what does “the gayatri and the peace chants” mean?
o: a well-known prayer for a lit mind and the peace chants, word by word
a lullaby families sing in Sanskrit to young children
a long list of blessings read aloud at a naming ceremony

games.q: the sage, the stuck king, the verse — tap the pairs.
p: pushed a king into the sky by force
prayers at the day's turning points

s: the Gayatri commands the god to stir our thoughts
prachodayat is a wish: may he stir. the verse asks.
in the Ramayana, Vishvamitra lifted Trishanku toward heaven by his own tapas
Indra pushed him back, and he was left hanging among new stars.
the Gayatri asks God for wealth and victory
it asks one thing: that the god stir our thoughts.

games.q: your nephew just had his sacred thread ceremony. he asks why the Gayatri doesn't ask God for anything useful, like good grades. which answer fits?
o: it asks for the mind itself to be lit, which comes before everything else you'd ask for.
it's too old to ask for anything; it's just a sound.
it does: prachodayat means may he make us win.
games.why: dhiyo yo nah prachodayat: may he stir our thoughts. many teachers read it as asking for the light to see by, before any wish, and asking, not forcing.

practice: Turn toward a window or the brightest light nearby. If the Gayatri is part of your practice, say it once, slowly, meaning the last word as a request. If not, hold its English in the light: may our thoughts be stirred.
Rest there until the time runs out.

wordCard.voice: The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: prachodayat, may he stir: the last word of a prayer that asks and doesn't force.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: prachodayat, may he urge on, the Gayatri's last word.

carryVoice: Your line: the Gayatri doesn't force; may he stir our minds. Ask for the light before you push. I'll be here tomorrow.
